To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Burkholderia pseudmallei can use ferritin iron for growth and virulence in mice.
B. pseudonallei is able to use iron from ferritin and hemoglobin in vitro and is still lethal in vivo in a mouse model of infection.
B. pseudomalei is a highly adaptable pathogen capable of utilizing a variety of iron sources, including a novel ferritin utilization system, to sustain in vivo infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the iron acquisition systems used by B. pseudomallelia and their contribution to virulence.
the identification and characterization of the iron acquisition system(s) of B. pseudomallelia.
the identification of the virulence determinants of B. pseudomollei, which are responsible for its ability to cause disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Burkholderia pseudmallei known siderophores and hemin uptake are dispensable for lethal murine meliodes.
B. pseudmallei is able to survive and proliferate in vivo in the absence of known siderophores, and that the siderophores are not required for virulence.
B. pseudonallei is not dependent on siderophore or hemin utilization for growth or pathogenesis in mice, although it can use siderophores, ferritin, hemoglobin, and hemin as an iron source.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the major known siderophores, hemin uptake locii, pyochelin uptake, malleobactins and ferritins are not required for B. pseudomallelis pathogenesis in mice.

B. pseudonallei can use multiple siderophore systems, and even a quadruple siderophore deletion mutant is able to cause disease in a murine model.
